Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, let $q_0\in\Omega$ with $\nabla U(q_0)=0$, and suppose $q_0$ is a **strict local minimum** of $U$: there is $r_0>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,r_0)\subseteq\Omega$ and

$$U(q)>U(q_0)\qquad(0<\|q-q_0\|_2<r_0).$$

Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]] on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, with energy $E(q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v+U(q)$. Then $(q_0,0)$ is a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of $(q',v')=G(q,v)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]: for every $\varepsilon>0$ with $\overline B((q_0,0),\varepsilon)\subseteq\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every maximal solution $(q,v)$ with $\|(q(0),v(0))-(q_0,0)\|_2<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|(q(t),v(t))-(q_0,0)\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

No asymptotic stability is asserted.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and let $E(q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v+U(q)$ be the energy of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]. If $q:I\to\Omega$ is a $C^2$ solution of the mechanical system $M(q)q''=\tfrac12\nabla_q(q'^{\mathsf T}M(q)q')-(D_qM(q)[q'])q'-\nabla U(q)$ on the interval $I$, then

$$\frac{d}{dt}E\bigl(q(t),q'(t)\bigr)=0\qquad(t\in I);$$

that is, the energy is constant along every solution.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and let $q_0\in\Omega$ be a mechanical equilibrium, that is $\nabla U(q_0)=0$ ([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]). Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$. Then:

1. $G$ is totally differentiable at $(q_0,0)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and, writing $D^2U(q_0)$ for the Hessian matrix ([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]),

$$DG(q_0,0)(\delta q,\delta v)=\Bigl(\delta v,\ -M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\delta q\Bigr)\qquad(\delta q,\delta v\in\mathbb R^n);$$

2. consequently the linearised equation at the equilibrium is

$$\xi''=-M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\xi,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad M(q_0)\xi''+D^2U(q_0)\,\xi=0,$$

a constant-coefficient system whose mass matrix $M(q_0)$ is symmetric positive definite and whose stiffness matrix $D^2U(q_0)$ is symmetric ([[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]);
3. if in addition $q_0$ is a strict local minimum of $U$, then $K:=D^2U(q_0)$ is non-negative, so the hypotheses of [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] are satisfied by $M(q_0)$ and $K$, and the linearised system is exactly the constant-coefficient quadratic system of that theorem with mass matrix $M(q_0)$ and stiffness $K$; its modes are the normal modes of the linearisation.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $0\in U$, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $F(0)=0$. Put $A:=DF(0)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and suppose that

- no complex eigenvalue of $A$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) has real part $0$, and
- at least one eigenvalue of $A$ has positive real part.

Then the equilibrium $0$ is not Lyapunov stable ([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]): there is a real number $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that for every $\delta>0$ there exist $z_0\in U$ with $\|z_0\|_2<\delta$ and a time $t_1>0$ such that the maximal solution $z$ of $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=z_0$ is defined on $[0,t_1]$ and satisfies

$$\|z(t_1)\|_2=\varepsilon_0 .$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Clause 2, spectral reduction: put $M_0:=M(q_0)$ and $S:=M_0^{-1/2}KM_0^{-1/2}$. Thus $-ho^2$ is an eigenvalue of $S$; as $S$ is negative definite, $-ho^2<0$, that is $ho^2>0$, so $ho$ is real and nonzero. Every complex eigenvalue of $A$ is therefore real and nonzero.

Clause 2, the growing solution: fix $j$ with $\lambda_j<0$, put $\kappa:=\sqrt{-\lambda_j}>0$ and $w:=M_0^{-1/2}u_j\ne0$. Then $Kw=\lambda_jM_0w$: indeed $Kw=KM_0^{-1/2}u_j=M_0^{1/2}M_0^{-1/2}KM_0^{-1/2}u_j=M_0^{1/2}Su_j=\lambda_jM_0^{1/2}u_j=\lambda_jM_0w$. Define $Y(t):=e^{\kappa t}(w,\kappa w)\in\mathbb R^{2n}$. By [L4], $Y_1'(t)=\kappa e^{\kappa t}w=Y_2(t)$ and $Y_2'(t)=\kappa^2e^{\kappa t}w=-\lambda_je^{\kappa t}w=-e^{\kappa t}M_0^{-1}Kw=-M_0^{-1}KY_1(t)$; by clause 1 of [L2] the map $Y$ therefore solves $Y'=DG(q_0,0)Y$ with $Y(0)=(w,\kappa w)$. Clause 3, instability: by [L3] second clause and the negativity of all eigenvalues of $S$, choose any eigenvalue $\lambda_j<0$ of $S$ with eigenvector $u_j$ and put $\kappa:=\sqrt{-\lambda_j}>0$, $w:=M_0^{-1/2}u_j$. Clause 4: [L1] second clause gives $E(z(t))=E(z(0))$ along every maximal solution. Suppose $(q_0,0)$ were asymptotically stable with attracting radius $\delta_0>0$ and let $z_0$ with $\lVert z_0-(q_0,0)\rVert_2<\delta_0$ and $E(z_0)\ne E(q_0,0)$, which exists by the clause's hypothesis. Its maximal solution is defined for all $t\ge0$ and converges to $(q_0,0)$; by the continuity of $E$ recorded in the Given, $E(z(t))\to E(q_0,0)$, while $E(z(t))=E(z_0)$ constantly, so $E(z_0)=E(q_0,0)$, a contradiction. Hence $(q_0,0)$ is not asymptotically stable. If $q_0$ is a strict local minimum with radius $r_0>0$, then for every $0<\lVert q-q_0\rVert_2<\min(\delta_0,r_0)$ the state $z_0:=(q,0)$ satisfies $E(z_0)=U(q)>U(q_0)=E(q_0,0)$, so such states accumulate at the equilibrium; combining clause 1 with the first part of this clause gives a Lyapunov stable but not asymptotically stable equilibrium.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $a_0\in U$, and let $T>0$, $R>0$ with $\overline B(a_0,R)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). Put $M:=\sup_{\overline B(a_0,R)}\|F\|_2$ and $L:=\sup_{\overline B(a_0,R)}\|DF\|$, where $DF(x)$ is the total derivative of $F$ at $x$ with its operator norm ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); both are finite. Let $0<\rho<R-MT$, so that in particular $MT<R$. Let $\Phi$ be the local flow of $x'=F(x)$ ([[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]).

Then:

1. For every $a\in\overline B(a_0,\rho)$ the maximal solution $x(\,\cdot\,;a)$ is defined on $[0,T]$ and satisfies $\|x(t;a)-a_0\|_2\le\rho+Mt<R$ for $t\in[0,T]$; moreover

$$\|x(t;a)-x(t;b)\|_2\le e^{Lt}\|a-b\|_2\qquad(a,b\in\overline B(a_0,\rho),\ t\in[0,T]),$$

and $(t,a)\mapsto x(t;a)$ is continuous on the compact set $[0,T]\times\overline B(a_0,\rho)$.

2. For every $a\in B(a_0,\rho)$ the variational equation along $x(\,\cdot\,;a)$,

$$Y'(t)=DF\bigl(x(t;a)\bigr)Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I_n,$$

has a unique solution $Y_a:[0,T]\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-variational-equation-along-an-ode-solution]]), and for every $t\in[0,T]$ the map $a\mapsto x(t;a)$ is differentiable on the open ball $B(a_0,\rho)$, with

$$D_a x(t;a)h=Y_a(t)h\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^n).$$

3. The map $(t,a)\mapsto Y_a(t)$ is continuous on $[0,T]\times B(a_0,\rho)$, and consequently $(t,a)\mapsto x(t;a)$ is $C^1$ there with

$$\partial_t x(t;a)=F\bigl(x(t;a)\bigr),\qquad D_a x(t;a)=Y_a(t).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $0\in U$, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $r>0$, $C\ge0$, $L\ge0$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\overline B(0,r)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) and

$$\|F(z)-Az\|_2\le C\|z\|_2^2,\qquad \|F(z)\|_2\le L\|z\|_2\qquad(\|z\|_2\le r).$$

Let $z_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\delta:=\|z_0\|_2>0$, let $T>0$ with $\delta e^{LT}<r$, and let $y:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be the solution of the linear system $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=z_0$ ([[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]]). Then:

1. The maximal solution $z$ of $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=z_0$ is defined on $[0,T]$ and satisfies $\|z(t)\|_2\le\delta e^{Lt}$ for $t\in[0,T]$ ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]).
2. For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|z(t)-y(t)\|_2\le C\delta^2\int_0^te^{\|A\|(t-s)}e^{2Ls}\,ds\le C\delta^2\,t\,e^{(\|A\|+2L)t},$$
where $\|A\|$ is the operator norm of $A$ for the Euclidean norm ([[def-operator-norm]]).

derivations.claim: Clause 1: the field $G$ is of class $C^1$ on $S_0$, because $M$ is $C^2$ and $U$ is $C^2$ ([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]); the numbers $M_R$ and $L_R$ are finite (continuous functions on the compact ball $\overline B(z_0,R)$). Apply [L1] with $F:=G$, $a_0:=z_0$, the given $R,T$ and $\rho$: every maximal solution through $a\in\overline B(z_0,\rho)$ is defined on $[0,T]$ and stays in $B(z_0,R)$, the Lipschitz bound $\lVert z(t;a)-z(t;b)\rVert_2\le e^{L_Rt}\lVert a-b\rVert_2$ holds, and $D_az(t;a)u=Y_a(t)u$ with $Y_a$ solving $Y'=DG(z(t;a))Y$, $Y(0)=I_{2n}$, which is exactly the variational equation along the model's motion through $a$.

Clause 3: put $U_0:=S_0-z_0$, an open neighborhood of $0$ containing $\overline B(0,r)$, and define $F:U_0\to\mathbb R^{2n}$ by $F(\zeta):=G(z_0+\zeta)$. Then $F$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state (the standing regularity of $G$), $F(0)=G(z_0)=0$, $DF(0)=DG(z_0)=A$, and the declared bounds are exactly the hypotheses of [L3] for $F$ with initial datum $a-z_0$ of norm $\delta$: $\lVert F(\zeta)-A\zeta\rVert_2\le C\lVert\zeta\rVert_2^2$ and $\lVert F(\zeta)\rVert_2\le L\lVert\zeta\rVert_2$ for $\lVert\zeta\rVert_2\le r$. Applying [L3] to $F$ and translating by $z_0$ gives exactly the displayed bound for $\lVert z(t;a)-z_0-y(t)\rVert_2$ with $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=a-z_0$, on the supplier's interval.

Clause 2: with $M$ constant, $G(q,v)=(v,-M^{-1}\nabla U(q))$ ([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]). By [L2], $\nabla U$ is differentiable with derivative $D^2U(q)$; hence $DG(q,v)(\delta q,\delta v)=(\delta v,-M^{-1}D^2U(q)\delta q)$. For the reference initial state $a$ of the Statement, write $Y_a=(Y_{a,q},Y_{a,v})$ in the variational equation of step 1.1. Then $Y_{a,q}'=Y_{a,v}$ and $Y_{a,v}'=-M^{-1}D^2U(q(t))Y_{a,q}$; eliminating the second block yields $M Y_{a,q}''=-D^2U(q(t))Y_{a,q}$, which is the displayed equation for $\eta=Y_{a,q}$, column by column.

Scope: clause 4 is the statement that no step above produced a conclusion outside the hypotheses of [L1] and [L3]: [L1] required the reference solution to stay in $\overline B(z_0,R)$ and yielded only the exponential Lipschitz bound, not an exact rate; [L3] required the quantitative bounds with constants $C,L,r$ and the smallness condition $\delta e^{LT}<r$; both are model-data hypotheses, and the constants are not measured quantities.

C2 kinetic metric/potential give a C1 field; compact closed R-ball gives finite suprema and rho<R-M_RT keeps each closed rho-ball trajectory inside the open R-ball. derivations.claim: Clause 1: the field $G$ is $C^1$ in the state by hypothesis, so $A=DG(z_*)$ is an endomorphism of $V=\mathbb R^{6N}$ with its Euclidean inner product; the hyperbolicity hypothesis is exactly the hypothesis of [L1] on the complexified eigenvalues. Applying [L1] with $T:=A$ gives the two invariant subspaces, the four exponential estimates and the two limit characterisations of clause 1.

Translation to the origin: define $U:=S_0-z_*=\{\zeta:\zeta+z_*\in S_0\}$, an open set containing $0$, and $F:U\to\mathbb R^{6N}$, $F(\zeta):=G(\zeta+z_*)$. Then $F$ is $C^1$, $F(0)=G(z_*)=0$, and $DF(0)=DG(z_*)=A$.

Clause 2: under the negative-spectrum hypothesis, [L2] applied to the field $F$ of step 1.2 gives $\delta,\beta,\gamma$ with $\lVert\zeta(t)\rVert_2\le\beta e^{-\gamma t}\lVert\zeta(0)\rVert_2$ for every maximal solution $\zeta$ of $\zeta'=F(\zeta)$ with $\lVert\zeta(0)\rVert_2<\delta$. The curves $t\mapsto\zeta(t)$ of $\zeta'=F(\zeta)$ are exactly the translates $z(t)-z_*$ of the model's maximal solutions through states near $z_*$, since $z'=G(z)$ iff $(z-z_*)'=G((z-z_*)+z_*)$; translating back gives the displayed bound and the all-$t\ge0$ domain of clause 2, and $[L2]$'s conclusion identifies it as Lyapunov and asymptotic stability in the sense of the model's stability vocabulary.

Clause 3: under the saddle hypothesis, [L3] applied to the field $F$ of step 1.2 yields $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that for every $\delta>0$ there are $\zeta_0$ with $\lVert\zeta_0\rVert_2<\delta$ and $t_1>0$ with $\lVert\zeta(t_1)\rVert_2=\varepsilon_0$; setting $z_0:=\zeta_0+z_*$ gives a model datum within distance $\delta$ of $z_*$ whose maximal solution leaves the ball of radius $\varepsilon_0$ at time $t_1$. Hence for every ball around $z_*$ there is a datum whose solution is not confined to a fixed ball of radius $\varepsilon_0$, so $z_*$ is not Lyapunov stable, that is unstable.

Clause 4: the constants and subspaces produced in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2 are those of [L1], [L2] and [L3] applied to the chart field $G$; a $C^2$ chart transition conjugates the derivative at $z_*$ by its Jacobian because $G(z_*)=0$, so the derivative matrices are similar and have the same spectrum ([[def-cm16-flow-equilibria-and-invariant-sets]] clause (vi)(b)). Throughout, fix an integer $n\ge1$. The space $\mathbb R^n$ is read through
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]] and $\mathbb C^n$ carries the polydisc
geometry of [[def-balls-and-polydiscs-in-complex-euclidean-space]]. All norms
below are supremum norms: for $z\in\mathbb C^m$,

$$|z|_\infty:=\max_{1\le i\le m}|z_i|,\qquad |z|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^m|z_i| .$$

**Angular torus.** Let $\mathbb Z$ be the integers ([[def-integers]]). Write
$k=(k_1,\dots,k_n)\in\mathbb Z^n$, $|k|_1=|k_1|+\dots+|k_n|$, and let
$(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\{2\pi k:k\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. On
$\mathbb R^n$ define the relation $\vartheta\sim\vartheta'$ by
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$. This is an equivalence relation, and
the **angular torus** is the quotient set

$$\mathbb T^n:=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^n:=\mathbb R^n/\!\sim$$

with the quotient topology ([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-product-topology]]),
and canonical projection $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb T^n$, which is continuous
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). A map $f:\mathbb R^n\to X$ is **$2\pi$-periodic** if
$f(\vartheta+2\pi k)=f(\vartheta)$ for all $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$; such an $f$ factors uniquely through $\pi$, and a map on
$\mathbb T^n$ is, by definition, a $2\pi$-periodic map on $\mathbb R^n$ read
through this factorisation. A function on $\mathbb T^n$ is **continuous**, resp.
**real analytic**, when its $2\pi$-periodic representative has that property.
Here **real analytic** has the componentwise meaning of
[[def-real-analytic-germ-in-several-variables]]: near every real point each real
component is represented by an absolutely convergent power series in the real
coordinates, and the same coefficients define a holomorphic function on a
complex polydisc whose restriction is the given real component. For a
vector-valued map this condition applies to each of its finitely many scalar
components.

**Action-angle neighbourhoods.** For $0<r$ and $0<s\le\infty$ put

$$B_r:=\{I\in\mathbb C^n:|I|_\infty<r\},\qquad S_s:=\{\vartheta\in\mathbb C^n:|\mathrm{Im}\,\vartheta|_\infty<s\},$$

and, for a set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (always measurably or
topologically qualified in the uses below) and $h\ge0$,

$$O_h(\Omega):=\{\nu\in\mathbb C^n:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega)<h\}, \qquad \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\nu,\Omega):=\inf_{\omega\in\Omega}|\nu-\omega|_\infty .$$

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ the infimum is taken in the extended nonnegative reals with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$, so $O_h(\varnothing)=\varnothing$ for every finite $h\ge0$. Supremum norms of functions on an empty domain are $0$ (the supremum in $[0,+\infty]$). Thus an empty Diophantine label set gives an empty parameter family; results quantified over its labels are vacuous, and positive-measure assertions require their separately stated hypotheses.

The **action-angle neighbourhood** of width $(r,s,h)$ over $\Omega$ is the open
product

$$D_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s\times O_h(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb C^{2n}\times\mathbb C^n,$$

and $D_{r,s}(\Omega):=B_r\times S_s$. In the KAM construction the parameter set
is a **frequency label set** $\Omega_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ (defined below)
and the relevant parameter neighbourhoods are $O_h(\Omega_\alpha)$; the
temperature of a step is measured by the three widths $r,s,h$ and an angular
margin $\sigma>0$.

**Holomorphic data and norms.** A function $g:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$
is **holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$** when it is continuous and separately
holomorphic in each of the $2n+n$ complex variables
([[def-separately-holomorphic-function]],
[[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]); equivalently, by
[[thm-power-series-expansion-in-several-complex-variables]], it is given near
every point by an absolutely convergent power series in the $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$
variables. The **sup-norms** are

$$|g|_{r,s}:=|g|_{r,s,0}:=\sup_{D_{r,s}(\Omega)}|g|,\qquad |g|_{r,s,h}:=|g|_{r,s,h}(\Omega):=\sup_{D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)}|g|\in[0,+\infty].$$

Where no parameter occurs we write $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$ if $g$ is holomorphic
on $D_{r,s}(\Omega)$ for some fixed open $\Omega$ and $|g|_{r,s}<+\infty$; and
$g\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ if $g$ is holomorphic on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ with
$|g|_{r,s,h}<+\infty$. Functions of $\vartheta$ alone are read through the
$2\pi$-periodicity of the $\vartheta$-variables, so that all integrals and
norms below are well defined on $\mathbb T^n$.

**Fourier coefficients, mean and cutoff.** Let $g\in\mathcal H_{r,s}$. For
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$ and $I\in B_r$ the **Fourier coefficient** is the iterated
Riemann integral

$$g_k(I):=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\cdots\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(I,\vartheta)\,e^{-ik\cdot\vartheta}\,d\vartheta_n\cdots d\vartheta_1 ,$$

as in [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]]; by
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] it equals the multiple Riemann
integral over $[0,2\pi]^n$ and is independent of the order of integration. The
**angular mean** of $g$ is $[g]:=g_0$, so $[g](I)=\frac1{(2\pi)^n}\int_{[0,2\pi]^n}g(I,\vartheta)\,d\vartheta$;
$g$ is **zero-mean** if $[g]=0$ for every $I\in B_r$. For a real number $K\ge0$
the **Fourier cutoff** $T_Kg$ is the trigonometric polynomial

$$T_Kg(I,\vartheta):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n,\ |k|_1\le K}g_k(I)\,e^{ik\cdot\vartheta}.$$

The sum is finite because $|k|_1\le K$ bounds each $|k_i|$ by $K$. For a
function $g$ of $(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ the same notations apply with the
$\nu$-variable carried along; e.g. $[g]$, $g_k$ and $T_Kg$ are then functions of
$(I,\nu)$.

**Frequency label sets.** Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\alpha>0$
and $\tau>n-1$. A frequency $\nu\in\mathbb R^n$ is **$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine**
if

$$|k\cdot\nu|\ge\alpha\,|k|_1^{-\tau}\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\},$$

with $k\cdot\nu=\sum_ik_i\nu_i$. The **label set** is

$$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}:=\Omega\cap\{\nu\in\mathbb R^n:\nu\text{ is }(\alpha,\tau)\text{-Diophantine}\}.$$

$\Omega_{\alpha,\tau}$ is closed in $\Omega$ and contained in the global
$(\alpha,\tau)$-Diophantine set; it need not have interior points. Write
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega$ when $\tau,\alpha$ are fixed and no confusion arises.
The parameter neighbourhoods used below are $O_h(\Omega_{\alpha,\tau})$.

**Hamiltonians, canonical form and Poisson bracket.** A **Hamiltonian datum**
on $D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)$ is a holomorphic $H:D_{r,s,h}(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ which
is real-valued on real points; more generally we consider families
$H(I,\vartheta;\nu)=e(\nu)+\nu\cdot I+P(I,\vartheta,\nu)$ where $e$ is
holomorphic on $O_h(\Omega)$ and real on real points, and
$P\in\mathcal H_{r,s,h}$ is real on real points. Pair the coordinates as
$q=\vartheta$, $p=I$ in the phase-domain notation of
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]; the **standard
two-form** in these coordinates is

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\vartheta_i\wedge dI_i,$$

and the **Hamiltonian vector field** of a $C^1$ Hamiltonian $H$ is, by
[[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] with
$(q,p)=(\vartheta,I)$,

$$X_H=(H_I,-H_\vartheta),\qquad \theta'=H_I,\quad I'=-H_\vartheta\ \ \text{(Hamilton's equations)},$$

characterised by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$; the **Poisson bracket** is

$$\{f,g\}=f_\vartheta\cdot g_I-f_I\cdot g_\vartheta,\qquad \{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g\ \ \text{in the notation of that item}.$$

In particular $\{f,e+\nu\cdot I\}=\nu\cdot f_\vartheta$ for every
$C^1$ function $f$.

**Angular parametrisations and Lagrangian images.** Fix a Hamiltonian datum
$H$. An **angular parametrisation** is a map $\psi=(\psi_I,\psi_\vartheta)$
with $\psi_I:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ $2\pi$-periodic and
$\psi_\vartheta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C^n$ satisfying
$\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta+2\pi k)=\psi_\vartheta(\vartheta)+2\pi k$ for all
$k\in\mathbb Z^n$, so that
$\pi\circ\psi_\vartheta=\pi\circ(\psi_\vartheta\big|_{\mathbb R^n})$ descends to
$\mathbb T^n$; it is **holomorphic on the strip $S_s$** when both components
extend holomorphically to $S_s$, and **real analytic** when in addition
$\psi(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the components are real analytic
in the real variables. It is **faithful** if
$\psi(\vartheta)=\psi(\vartheta')$ implies
$\vartheta-\vartheta'\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^n$, and an **immersion** if
$D\psi(\vartheta)$ has rank $n$ for every $\vartheta\in\mathbb R^n$; a tuple
that is both is an **embedded torus parametrisation**. Its image is
**Lagrangian** (with respect to $\omega$) if
$\psi^*\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d(\psi_\vartheta)_i\wedge d(\psi_I)_i=0$ as a
two-form on the parameter space of the representative, and **invariant with
frequency $\nu$** if

$$X_H(\psi(\vartheta))=\sum_{j=1}^n\nu_j\,\partial_{\vartheta_j}\psi(\vartheta) \qquad\text{for all real }\vartheta .$$

2. A point $x\in X$ is a **periodic point** of $f$ when $f^n(x)=x$ for some $n\ge1$. The set of periodic points of $f$ is written $\operatorname{Per}(f)$. The periodic points are **dense** in $X$ when $\operatorname{Per}(f)$ is dense in $X$, that is ([[def-dense-top]]) when every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $\operatorname{Per}(f)$.

3. $f$ has **sensitive dependence on initial conditions** when there is a real number $\delta>0$ such that for every $x\in X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $y\in X$ and $n\ge1$ with

$$d(x,y)<\varepsilon\qquad\text{and}\qquad d\bigl(f^n(x),f^n(y)\bigr)\ge\delta .$$

Such a number $\delta$ is called a **sensitivity constant** for $f$.

Finally, say that $f$ is **chaotic in the stated sense** when $f$ is continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]), topologically mixing, has dense periodic points, and has sensitive dependence on initial conditions.

momentum charts and two-form datum of [[def-cm13-two-form]], the canonical
coordinates of [[def-cm13-canonical-form]], the canonical maps of
[[def-cm13-canonical-map]] and the Hamiltonian field of
[[def-cm13-hamiltonian-field]]: the Cartesian Hamiltonian
$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x)$ of class $C^{2}$ on
$I_{0}\times W$, where the potential $U$ and the residual forces $d$ are
those of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and the data are those of
[[def-cm01-configuration]], [[def-cm01-units]]
([[def-cm12-hamiltonian]], [[pthm-cm12-mechanical-hyperregularity]]). Let
$t_{0}\in I_{0}$ and $z_{0}\in W$. Then there are reals $h>0$, $\rho>0$ and
an open neighbourhood $U_{0}\subseteq W$ of $z_{0}$ such that:

   system $\dot z(t)=X_{H_{t}}(z(t))$ through $y\in U_{0}$ at time $t_{0}$
   are defined for $t\in[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]$, and the solution map
   $\Phi:[t_{0}-h,t_{0}+h]\times U_{0}\to W$ is $C^{1}$ in $y$; for each
   fixed $t$ the time-$t$ map $\Phi_{t}:=\Phi(t;\cdot)$ is a canonical map
   of the presentation between equal-dimensional phase domains, and thus a
   local canonical transformation on $U_{0}$:

$$D\Phi_{t}(y)^{\mathsf T}J\,D\Phi_{t}(y)=J,\qquad \Phi_{t}^{*}\omega=\omega\qquad(y\in U_{0}),$$

   and $\det D\Phi_{t}(y)=1$ for every $y\in U_{0}$.

   $C^{2}$ phase functions $f,g$ on $W$,

   $C^{1}$ compositions defined in [[def-cm13-poisson]].

   $t\mapsto\Phi(t;y)$ are, through
   [[pthm-cm13-hamiltonian-field-integrates-the-model-equations]], the

   evolution preserves the presentation's two-form, bracket and determinant

[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], [[def-cm01-configuration]],

$$\Omega:=\frac{1}{n!}\,\omega^{\wedge n}$$

has the same phase-volume unit. By
[[cor-symplectic-manifolds-have-a-canonical-orientation-and-volume-form]]
applied to the symplectic phase domain of
[[pthm-cm13-two-form-is-symplectic]], $\Omega$ is a nowhere-zero top form

   $\Phi_{t}^{*}\Omega=\Omega$ on $U_{0}$; the time slices of the model's
   Hamiltonian evolution preserve the phase-volume form.
2. **(measure preservation)** For every $t$ on the existence interval and
   every bounded Borel set $A\subseteq U_{0}$ with
   $\overline A\subseteq U_{0}$, the sets $A$ and $\Phi_{t}(A)$ are
   Lebesgue measurable and

$$\lambda_{6N}\bigl(\Phi_{t}(A)\bigr)=\lambda_{6N}(A),$$

   where $\lambda_{6N}$ is the Lebesgue measure of the chart
   ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]],
   [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]],
   [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]).

   full-dimensional canonical chart: for two genuine $6N$-dimensional phase

   overlap and a Borel set $B$ of finite measure in its domain,

   equal-dimensional canonical transformation has $|\det D\Theta|=1$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $a_0\in U$, and let $T>0$, $R>0$ with $\overline B(a_0,R)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). $$\|x(t;a)-x(t;b)\|_2\le e^{Lt}\|a-b\|_2\qquad(a,b\in\overline B(a_0,\rho),\ t\in[0,T]),$$

and $(t,a)\mapsto x(t;a)$ is continuous on the compact set $[0,T]\times\overline B(a_0,\rho)$.

$$Y'(t)=DF\bigl(x(t;a)\bigr)Y(t),\qquad Y(0)=I_n,$$

has a unique solution $Y_a:[0,T]\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-variational-equation-along-an-ode-solution]]), and for every $t\in[0,T]$ the map $a\mapsto x(t;a)$ is differentiable on the open ball $B(a_0,\rho)$, with

$$D_a x(t;a)h=Y_a(t)h\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^n).$$

3. The map $(t,a)\mapsto Y_a(t)$ is continuous on $[0,T]\times B(a_0,\rho)$, and consequently $(t,a)\mapsto x(t;a)$ is $C^1$ there with

$$\partial_t x(t;a)=F\bigl(x(t;a)\bigr),\qquad D_a x(t;a)=Y_a(t).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

happens at $n = 0$.

One short time slice preserves volume on every Borel subset of $A$: fix $|s|\le h$ and a Borel set $B\subseteq A$. The images are pairwise disjoint because $\Phi_s$ is injective on $A$, with inverse $\Phi_{-s}|_A$; they lie in $A$ by invariance. $$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$

([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;

   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis

no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.

followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: The two fields: for the constant metric $M=I_3$ the mechanical field of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]] is $G(\mathbf q,\mathbf v)=(\mathbf v,-\nabla U(\mathbf q))$, giving $G_1(\mathbf q,\mathbf v)=(\mathbf v,-\mathbf q)$ and $G_2(\mathbf q,\mathbf v)=(\mathbf v,\mathbf q)$. These are also the force-model fields of the declared $F_1,F_2$.

Harmonic flow: differentiating the displayed $\Phi_t^1$ with respect to $t$ by [L2] gives $(\dot{\mathbf q},\dot{\mathbf v})=(\mathbf v,-\mathbf q)$; at $t=0$ the map is the identity. By [L1] the displayed map is the force model's maximal flow.

Repulsive flow: differentiating the displayed $\Phi_t^2$ gives $\dot{\mathbf q}=\mathbf v(t)$ and $\dot{\mathbf v}=\mathbf q(t)$; at $t=0$ the map is the identity, so by [L1] it is the force model's maximal flow of $G_2$.

Harmonic growth rates: $\Phi_t^1$ is linear in $a=(\mathbf q_0,\mathbf v_0)$, with derivative $$D_a\Phi_t^1(a)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t\,I_3&\sin t\,I_3\\-\sin t\,I_3&\cos t\,I_3\end{pmatrix};$$ this matrix is orthogonal, whence $\lVert D_a\Phi_t^1(a)u\rVert_2=\lVert u\rVert_2$ for every $u\ne0$. The explicit flow exists for every real time, so the forward lifetime is unbounded, as required by the exponent definition. Therefore $r(t,a,u)=t^{-1}\log1=0$ for every $t>0$, and the limit defining the Lyapunov exponent exists and equals $0$; the variational equation of [[pthm-cm16-variational-equation-and-linearization]] is satisfied by this derivative matrix, whose columns solve $\dot Y=DG_1Y$ by step 2.1.

For each $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, input $(\mathbf e_j,\mathbf e_j)$ gives output $e^t(\mathbf e_j,\mathbf e_j)$ and rate $+1$, while input $(\mathbf e_j,-\mathbf e_j)$ gives output $e^{-t}(\mathbf e_j,-\mathbf e_j)$ and rate $-1$. At the equilibrium $a=(\mathbf 0,\mathbf 0)$ this gives a positive exponent along each unstable coordinate eigenvector.

and velocity $\mathbf v=\dot{\mathbf r}\in\mathbb R^3$ for one label of mass
$m$. The adopted force map on
$\mathbb R\times Q_{\mathrm{conf}}\times\mathbb R^3$ is
$$\mathbf F(T,\mathbf r,\mathbf v):=-m\omega_0^2\Bigl(Q+\ell_0\beta_\delta(\omega_0T)\Bigl(a-\frac{Q^2}{\ell_0^2}\Bigr),\ -Y,\ -Z\Bigr),\qquad T_p:=\frac{P}{\omega_0}.$$

a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with fixed mass $m$; its
motions are the $C^2$ curves of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The phase plane
$$\mathcal P:=\{(\mathbf r,\mathbf v):Y=Z=v_Y=v_Z=0\}$$
is invariant. Define canonical momenta $\boldsymbol\Pi:=m\mathbf v=
(\Pi_Q,\Pi_Y,\Pi_Z)$, with axial component $\Pi:=\Pi_Q$. The restricted equation is
$$m\ddot Q=-m\omega_0^2\Bigl[Q+\ell_0\beta_\delta(\omega_0T)\Bigl(a-\frac{Q^2}{\ell_0^2}\Bigr)\Bigr].$$

[[def-cm16-stroboscopic-and-poincare-maps]] clause (i).

[[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]] onto a compact subset

$$\Psi_\delta\circ H_\delta=H_\delta\circ S_\pm.$$

conjugate to the shift; with the Euclidean metric inherited from the full
phase chart it is chaotic in the stated sense of
[[def-cm16-chaos-list-for-model-maps]]: continuous, topologically mixing, with
dense periodic points and sensitive dependence with a positive constant.

$\mathcal U_\delta,\mathcal V_\delta\subseteq\mathbb R^6$ with

sequence $\bar u$. Define the
stable and unstable sets for the stated branch by
$$W^s(z_*):=\{z\in\mathcal U_\delta:\Psi_\delta^n(z)\in\mathcal U_\delta\text{ for every }n\ge0\text{ and }\Psi_\delta^n(z)\to z_*\},$$
$$W^u(z_*):=\{z\in\mathcal V_\delta:\Psi_\delta^{-n}(z)\in\mathcal V_\delta\text{ for every }n\ge0\text{ and }\Psi_\delta^{-n}(z)\to z_*\},$$

map $F_0$ has domain
$D_0:=I_0\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, exactly as in clause (iii) of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]. The page may specify an open restriction
domain $D\subseteq D_0$ and then uses $F:=F_0|_D$; every force evaluation in
the statements below is on this restriction. This is still a restriction of
the supplier's full force map, not a force map with a different domain. The
**motions** are the $C^2$ curves $x:J\to Q$ of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]
for which $(t,x(t),x'(t))\in D$ and
$m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$. For a proper restriction $D$, call such a
motion **$D$-maximal** when it has no extension to a strictly larger interval
whose state curve remains in $D$; this is the maximal-solution notion for the
first-order ODE $z'=Z(t,z)$ on the open domain $D$
([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]],
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]). A $D$-maximal motion is a restriction of a
supplier motion of the full force model, but its maximal interval need not be
maximal for the full domain $D_0$. The model is **autonomous** when
$I_0=\mathbb R$, $D=\mathbb R\times S_0$ for an open **state domain**
$S_0\subseteq Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, and $F$ is independent of $t$. It is
**$P$-periodic**, for $P>0$, when $I_0=\mathbb R$, $D$ is invariant under
$(t,x,v)\mapsto(t+P,x,v)$ in both directions, and
$F(t+P,x,v)=F(t,x,v)$ on $D$. Thus every integer shift by $P$ preserves the
time and state domain used by the model. All time intervals use the frame-time
parameter fixed by [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]] with $[t]=\tau$
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(ii) Associated field and flow.** Write $n:=3N$,
$\mathsf M:=\operatorname{diag}(m_1I_3,\dots,m_NI_3)$, and let
$$Z(t,x,v):=\bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\bigr)$$
be the **associated first-order field** of the model, on the same domain $D$;
the state curve $z:=(x,x')$ of a motion is a solution of $z'=Z(t,z)$ and
conversely ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]] clause (c)). For an autonomous model
write $G:S_0\to\mathbb R^{6N}$, $G(x,v):=(v,\mathsf M^{-1}F(x,v))$; by the
standing regularity of $F$, the field $G$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz
in the state, so it has a **local flow**
$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow S_0,\qquad \Phi(t,z_0):=z(t;z_0),$$
with maximal solutions $z(\,\cdot\,;z_0):I_{z_0}\to S_0$ and flow domain
$\Omega=\{(t,z_0):t\in I_{z_0}\}$, in the sense of
[[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]. The model's motions with state
curve through $z_0$ at time $0$ are exactly the curves $t\mapsto\Phi(t,z_0)$
restricted to their maximal intervals, and
$\Phi(s+t,z_0)=\Phi(t,\Phi(s,z_0))$ wherever both sides are defined
([[lem-cm-local-flow-composition-law]]). If in addition $F$ is of class $C^1$
in the state, then $\Omega$ is open and $\Phi$ is $C^1$ on it
([[cor-cm-flow-domain-open-and-flow-is-c1]]). No completeness of $\Phi$ is
asserted: the maximal interval $I_{z_0}$ may be bounded
([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]).

**(iii) Equilibria and periodic orbits.** A state $z_*=(x_*,v_*)\in S_0$ is an
**equilibrium state** of the autonomous model when $G(z_*)=0$, that is
$v_*=0$ and $F(x_*,0)=0$; under that condition the constant curve
$x(t)=x_*$ is a motion. A **periodic motion** of the model is a nonconstant
motion $x:\mathbb R\to Q$ satisfying $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for every
$t\in\mathbb R$ and some $T>0$; the least such positive $T$ is its **least
period**. Its state curve is $z(t):=(x(t),x'(t))$, and its **state orbit** is
$\Gamma_z:=\{z(t):t\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq S_0$. A **periodic orbit** or
**closed orbit** means this state orbit. A **limit cycle** is an isolated
periodic orbit: there is an open set $U\subseteq S_0$ with
$\Gamma_z\subseteq U$ such that every periodic orbit $\Gamma_{\widetilde z}$
of this model satisfying $\Gamma_{\widetilde z}\subseteq U$ equals
$\Gamma_z$. Thus $U$ contains no other periodic orbit as a whole; an orbit
that merely passes through $U$ is not excluded. A limit cycle's attraction is
a separate property and is not part of this definition.

**(iv) Invariant sets.** A set $S\subseteq S_0$ is **invariant** for the
autonomous model when $(t,z)\in\Omega$ for every $z\in S$ and every
$t\in\mathbb R$, and $\Phi_t(S)=S$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$, where
$\Phi_t(z):=\Phi(t,z)$; it is **forward invariant** when $(t,z)\in\Omega$ for
every $z\in S$, $t\ge0$, and $\Phi_t(S)\subseteq S$ for every $t\ge0$. The
**orbital distance** from a state $z$ to a nonempty set $S$ is
$$d(z,S):=\inf_{s\in S}\lVert z-s\rVert_2,$$
with the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the state
chart.

**(v) Homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits.** A nonconstant motion with state
curve $z$ is **homoclinic to** an equilibrium state $z_*$ when $z(t)\to z_*$ as
$t\to+\infty$ and as $t\to-\infty$, and is **heteroclinic from $z_-$ to
$z_+$** for distinct equilibrium states $z_-,z_+$ when $z(t)\to z_-$ as
$t\to-\infty$ and $z(t)\to z_+$ as $t\to+\infty$. Both are limit relations
of the model's motions, not intersections of separately constructed geometric
objects; the differentiability of the associated stable and unstable sets is
not asserted here.

**(vi) Reading conventions.** (a) The vocabulary is attached to the declared
model class; equilibria, periodic orbits, invariant sets and homoclinic orbits
are model objects, and no clause asserts that a physical system is exactly a
stability model or realises any of these objects. (b) The state space is
written in a Cartesian chart. If a $C^2$ chart transition $h$ changes an
autonomous field from $G$ to $\widetilde G(h(z))=Dh(z)G(z)$, then at an
equilibrium $z_*$ its derivative satisfies
$D\widetilde G(h(z_*))=Dh(z_*)DG(z_*)Dh(z_*)^{-1}$: the term differentiating
$Dh$ vanishes because $G(z_*)=0$. Thus the linearization spectrum at an
equilibrium is chart-invariant. Norms, matrix entries and quantitative growth
bounds can still depend on the chart; the underlying motions, equilibria,
periodic orbits, invariant sets and their asymptotic properties do not change
under a valid coordinate description.

Let an autonomous stability model be fixed whose force map is of class $C^1$
in the state, with state domain $S_0\subseteq\mathbb R^{6N}$, associated
$C^1$ field $G$ and local flow
$\Phi:\Omega\to S_0$ ([[def-cm16-flow-equilibria-and-invariant-sets]] clauses
(i)-(ii)); all differentiability is that of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Let $z_*\in S_0$ be an
equilibrium state, $G(z_*)=0$, and let
$A:=DG(z_*)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]). Then:

1. **(Exponential dichotomy.)** If no complex eigenvalue of $A$
   ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) has real part
   $0$ --- that is, if $z_*$ is hyperbolic in the sense of
   [[def-cm16-stability-and-hyperbolicity-concepts]] clause (iv) --- then
   there are $A$-invariant subspaces $E_s,E_u\subseteq\mathbb R^{6N}$ with
   $\mathbb R^{6N}=E_s\oplus E_u$ and real constants $C\ge1$, $c>0$ such
   that, with the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the
   exponential series $e^{tA}$:
   $$\lVert e^{tA}v\rVert_2\le Ce^{-ct}\lVert v\rVert_2\ (v\in E_s,\ t\ge0), \qquad \lVert e^{tA}v\rVert_2\ge C^{-1}e^{ct}\lVert v\rVert_2\ (v\in E_u,\ t\ge0),$$
   $$\lVert e^{tA}v\rVert_2\le Ce^{ct}\lVert v\rVert_2\ (v\in E_u,\ t\le0),$$
   and $E_s=\{v:e^{tA}v\to0\ (t\to+\infty)\}$,
   $E_u=\{v:e^{tA}v\to0\ (t\to-\infty)\}$. The spaces $E_s,E_u$ are the
   **stable and unstable subspaces** of the linearised flow.
2. **(Stable case.)** If every complex eigenvalue of $A$ has negative real
   part, then $z_*$ is locally exponentially asymptotically stable: there are
   $\delta>0$, $\beta\ge1$, $\gamma>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$
   of the model with $\lVert z(0)-z_*\rVert_2<\delta$ is defined for all
   $t\ge0$ and satisfies
   $$\lVert z(t)-z_*\rVert_2\le\beta e^{-\gamma t}\lVert z(0)-z_*\rVert_2\qquad(t\ge0).$$
   In particular $z_*$ is Lyapunov stable and asymptotically stable
   ([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]).
3. **(Saddle case.)** If no complex eigenvalue of $A$ has real part $0$ and
   at least one has positive real part, then $z_*$ is unstable: there is
   $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that for every $\delta>0$ there are a state $z_0$
   with $\lVert z_0-z_*\rVert_2<\delta$ and a time $t_1>0$ such that the
   maximal solution through $z_0$ is defined on $[0,t_1]$ and
   $\lVert z(t_1)-z_*\rVert_2=\varepsilon_0$.
4. **(Rates, charts and scope.)** The constants $C,c,\beta,\gamma$ and the
   coordinate descriptions of the subspaces depend on the chosen chart and
   norm; the rates $c,\gamma$ have dimension $\tau^{-1}$. Under a smooth
   change of chart the derivative matrices at the equilibrium are similar, so
   their eigenvalue spectrum is invariant, while the Euclidean estimates may
   change as recorded in [[def-cm16-stability-and-hyperbolicity-concepts]]
   clause (vi)(b). No conclusion is asserted when some eigenvalue has zero real part
   (the centre case), and no statement is made about the size of the stable
   set, the basin of attraction, uniformity in a family of models or any
   empirical realization.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let
$M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite
matrices, and let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$; let $G$ be the
mechanical vector field and $E(q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v+U(q)$ the
energy of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]. Let
$q_0\in\Omega$ be a mechanical equilibrium, $\nabla U(q_0)=0$, and put
$K:=D^2U(q_0)$ ([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]],
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]). Then:

1. **(Strict minimum.)** If $q_0$ is a strict local minimum of $U$, then
   $(q_0,0)$ is a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of $G$
   ([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]],
   [[def-cm16-stability-and-hyperbolicity-concepts]] clause (i)).
2. **(Linear instability from a negative eigenvalue.)** If $K$ has a negative
   eigenvalue ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), then
   there are $\mu>0$ and $w\ne0$ in $\mathbb R^n$ such that
   $t\mapsto e^{\mu t}(w,\mu w)$ is a solution of the variational equation
   $Y'=DG(q_0,0)Y$ along the constant solution $z\equiv(q_0,0)$
   ([[def-variational-equation-along-an-ode-solution]]); in particular
   $(q_0,0)$ is linearly unstable in the sense of
   [[def-cm16-stability-and-hyperbolicity-concepts]] clause (iii).
3. **(Nonlinear instability from a strictly concave potential.)** If $K$ is
   negative definite, then every complex eigenvalue of $DG(q_0,0)$ is real
   and nonzero, at least one is positive, and $(q_0,0)$ is unstable: it is
   not Lyapunov stable.
4. **(No attraction under exact energy conservation.)** The energy $E$ is
   constant along every maximal solution of $G$. If there are states
   $z=(q,v)$ with $\lVert z-(q_0,0)\rVert_2$ arbitrarily small and
   $E(z)\ne E(q_0,0)$, then $(q_0,0)$ is not asymptotically stable. In
   particular, if $q_0$ is a strict local minimum of $U$, then $(q_0,0)$ is
   Lyapunov stable but not asymptotically stable.
5. **(Scope.)** No statement is made about a degenerate Hessian $K$ (some
   eigenvalue $0$), and clause 2 gives no nonlinear conclusion when $K$ has
   both a negative and a positive eigenvalue: the linearisation then also has
   purely imaginary eigenvalues and is not hyperbolic, so the instability
   theorem used in clause 3 does not apply. No global stability, no basin of
   attraction and no statement about the size of any neighbourhood is
   claimed.

This item attaches stability predicates to two explicitly stated model
classes. **(a) Framework force models:** an autonomous model of
[[def-cm16-flow-equilibria-and-invariant-sets]] clauses (i)-(ii), with open
state domain $S_0\subseteq\mathbb R^{6N}$, associated field
$G:S_0\to\mathbb R^{6N}$ and its maximal-solution local flow
$\Phi:\Omega\to S_0$ ([[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]).
**(b) Mechanical chart models:** the data $(\Omega,M,U)$ of
[[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]], where
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is open, $M$ is a $C^2$ positive-definite
matrix field, and $U$ is $C^2$; here the state domain is
$S_0:=\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, the state dimension is $m:=2n$, and the
associated mechanical field is $G:S_0\to\mathbb R^m$. It is $C^1$, hence
continuous and locally Lipschitz, and has the local flow and maximal solutions
of [[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]. For class (a) only the
standing continuous, state-locally-Lipschitz regularity is required for
clauses (i)-(ii); clauses (iii)-(iv) add $C^1$ regularity explicitly. In each
application the predicates concern the declared model objects and quantify
over its maximal solutions; the two model classes are not being identified.

**(i) Lyapunov and asymptotic stability.** Let $z_*\in S_0$ be an equilibrium
state. The state $z_*$ is **Lyapunov stable** when for every Euclidean ball
$B_\varepsilon(z_*)$ with $\overline{B_\varepsilon(z_*)}\subseteq S_0$
([[def-metric-ball]]) there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every
maximal solution $z$ with $\lVert z(0)-z_*\rVert_2<\delta$ is defined for all
$t\ge0$ and satisfies $\lVert z(t)-z_*\rVert_2<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge0$.
It is **asymptotically stable** when it is Lyapunov stable and there is
$\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution with
$\lVert z(0)-z_*\rVert_2<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and converges to
$z_*$ as $t\to\infty$. This is the definition of
[[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] clauses 1-2, applied to the
autonomous field $G$ on $S_0$; it is recorded here to fix the exact
quantifier order and the requirement that the solutions are defined for all
$t\ge0$. A state that is not Lyapunov stable is **unstable**.

**(ii) Orbital stability of an invariant set.** Let $S\subseteq S_0$ be a
nonempty compact set invariant under the selected model's local flow $\Phi$;
that is, $(t,z)\in\Omega$ for every $z\in S$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, and
$\Phi_t(S)=S$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$. For the framework force-model
class this is clause (iv) of
[[def-cm16-flow-equilibria-and-invariant-sets]]. The Euclidean orbital
distance is $d(z,S):=\inf_{s\in S}\lVert z-s\rVert_2$. Then $S$ is
**orbitally stable** when for every open set
$U\supseteq S$ there is an open set $V$ with $S\subseteq V\subseteq U$ such
that every maximal solution $z$ with $z(0)\in V$ is defined for all $t\ge0$
and satisfies $z(t)\in U$ for all $t\ge0$. Orbital stability is a statement
about the set, not about one motion, and it does not assert attraction.

**(iii) Linear stability of an equilibrium.** Suppose the field $G$ of the
chosen model is of class $C^1$ on its state domain $S_0$, so that its local
flow is $C^1$ and $DG(z_*)$ exists. Write $m:=\dim S_0$. For each initial
deviation $u\in\mathbb R^m$, let $\eta_u:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m$ be the unique
solution of the constant-coefficient variational equation
$$\eta_u'(t)=DG(z_*)\eta_u(t),\qquad \eta_u(0)=u$$
([[def-variational-equation-along-an-ode-solution]], with the constant
solution $z(t)=z_*$ as the reference motion). The equilibrium $z_*$ is
**linearly stable** when
$\sup_{t\ge0}\lVert\eta_u(t)\rVert_2<\infty$ for every $u$; it is
**linearly unstable** if this norm is unbounded as $t\to\infty$ for some
$u$. This is a statement about the linear variational equation and is distinct
from the nonlinear Lyapunov and asymptotic predicates in clause (i).

**(iv) Hyperbolicity of an equilibrium.** Let $z_*$ be an equilibrium state
of the chosen autonomous model whose associated field $G$ is $C^1$ on $S_0$,
and let $DG(z_*)$ be its derivative. Then $z_*$ is
**hyperbolic** when no complex eigenvalue of $DG(z_*)$
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) has real part $0$;
the eigenvalues are those of the matrix of $DG(z_*)$ in the state chart. The
harmonic oscillator equilibrium of a one-dimensional model with a positive
stiffness has the purely imaginary eigenvalues $\pm i\omega$ and is therefore
not hyperbolic; the saddle of a repulsive linear model has the real
eigenvalues $\pm\mu$, $\mu>0$, and is hyperbolic.

**(v) Linear stability and hyperbolicity of a map.** Let $X,Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open and let $\Psi:X\to Y$ be of class $C^1$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A **fixed point** of this
local map is a point $a\in X$ with $\Psi(a)=a\in Y$. The fixed point is
**linearly stable** when $\sup_{n\ge0}\lVert D\Psi(a)^nu\rVert_2<\infty$ for
every $u\in\mathbb R^m$, and **hyperbolic** when no complex eigenvalue of
$D\Psi(a)$ has modulus $1$. These predicates require only the local map near
the fixed point; they concern its derivative, not its nonlinear iterates on
everywhere-defined state domains.

**(vi) Distinctions.** (a) The predicates in clauses (i)-(v) have different
definitions and are not interchangeable. In particular, Lyapunov stability
does not by definition include attraction, and orbital stability is a
property of a set rather than of one of its points. Hyperbolicity alone does
not imply linear instability: if all eigenvalues of $DG(z_*)$ have negative
real part, the stable estimate of
[[thm-cm-exponential-dichotomy-for-a-hyperbolic-endomorphism]] makes every
solution of the variational equation decay and hence remain bounded. If a
hyperbolic equilibrium has an eigenvalue with positive real part, the same
dichotomy supplies an unbounded forward solution and the equilibrium is
linearly unstable. (b) At
an equilibrium the spectrum of $DG(z_*)$ is invariant under a $C^2$ chart
transition, by the similarity formula in
[[def-cm16-flow-equilibria-and-invariant-sets]] clause (vi)(b); norms and
finite-time growth bounds can depend on the chart. (c) For the
mechanical chart data $(M,U)$ of
[[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]], at a mechanical
equilibrium $(q_0,0)$ the derivative of the field is
$DG(q_0,0)(\delta q,\delta v)=(\delta v,-M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\delta q)$; the
stability consequences of that computation are proved later on the page.

Adopt the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]: the
one-dimensional model of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]
with $m>0$, $k>0$, force law $F(x)=-kx$ and potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$.
Write
$$\omega:=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}>0$$
for its **undamped frequency** in the sense of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]. Then:

1. **Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
   interior and let $t_{0}\in J$. A curve $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a motion of the
   model on $J$ if and only if there are reals $A,B$ with
   $$x(t)=A\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr)+B\sin\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})\bigr) \qquad(t\in J).$$
   For every datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is exactly one maximal motion,
   it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and its coefficients are
   $A=x_{0}$, $B=v_{0}/\omega$; every motion with that datum is its
   restriction.
All claims involving every real time, periods or the whole phase ellipse below refer to the unique maximal extension of clause 1; on a local motion interval the same formulas hold by restriction.

2. **Amplitude and phase.** With $A,B$ as in clause 1 put
   $R:=\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}$. Then $\lvert x(t)\rvert\le R$ for every $t$; if
   $R>0$ there is a real $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi=A/R$ and
   $\sin\varphi=B/R$, and then
   $$x(t)=R\cos\bigl(\omega(t-t_{0})-\varphi\bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
   If $R=0$ the motion is the rest motion $x\equiv0$.
3. **Period and frequency.** For every motion $x(t+T)=x(t)$ holds for all
   $t$ whenever $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. If $R>0$, conversely every
   period $T>0$ of $x$ satisfies $\omega T\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, so the **least
   positive period** of the motion is $T_{\mathrm{per}}=2\pi/\omega$, and the
   **frequency** in cycles per second is $f=1/T_{\mathrm{per}}=\omega/(2\pi)$.
   If $R=0$ every $T$ is a period.
4. **Energy and phase curves.** Along every motion with coefficients $A,B$
   the mechanical energy is
   $$E\bigl(x(t),x'(t)\bigr)=\tfrac12k\bigl(A^{2}+B^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12kR^{2}$$
   for every $t$, the phase curve is contained in the ellipse
   $$\Sigma_{R}:=\Bigl\{(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{2}:\frac{x^{2}}{R^{2}}+\frac{v^{2}}{\omega^{2}R^{2}}=1\Bigr\}$$
   when $R>0$, and it is exactly that ellipse: every point of $\Sigma_{R}$
   lies on the phase curve of the motion and is attained at exactly the times
   $t=t_{0}+\bigl(\theta_{1}+\varphi+2\pi n\bigr)/\omega$, $n\in\mathbb Z$,
   for the appropriate $\theta_{1}$. For $R=0$ the phase curve is the single
   point $(0,0)$, which is also the level set of energy $0$.
5. **Rest point.** The origin $(0,0)$ is the only rest point of the model,
   and it is Lyapunov stable, by
   [[pthm-cm04-equilibrium-stability-at-a-strict-minimum]]; no asymptotic
   stability is asserted.

The statement uses the declared data $m,k$ only through $\omega$ and the
energy; no value of $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and no real oscillator is claimed
to obey the model.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from the phase-volume preservation
theorem [[pthm-cm13-liouville]] (its measure-preservation clause uses the
change-of-variables theorem under that assumption). Adopt the force model with
potential presentation and the Hamiltonian data of [[pthm-cm13-liouville]]:
time-independent potential $U:Q\to\mathbb R$ with residual forces
$d\equiv0$, Cartesian phase domain $W=Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm13-two-form]]), Hamiltonian
$$H:I_0\times W\to\mathbb R,\qquad H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(x),$$
phase-volume form $\Omega=\omega^{\wedge3N}/(3N)!$. Let $A\subseteq W$ be a
bounded Borel set ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) whose closure is contained in
the open phase domain $W$. Let $\Phi_t$ denote the potential-branch flow on
its maximal time-slice domain, and suppose it is defined at every point of $A$
for all real times and maps $A$ onto itself:
$$\Phi_t(A)=A\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
so that $A$ is invariant in the sense of
[[def-cm16-flow-equilibria-and-invariant-sets]] clause (iv). Then
$\lambda_{6N}(A)<\infty$, and the flow preserves $\lambda_{6N}$ on every
Borel subset of $A$, by the finite-cover and time-subdivision argument in the
proof below. For every Borel set $E\subseteq A$ almost every
$x\in E$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{6N}$ of the chart
([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]) has
$$\Phi_n(x)\in E\qquad\text{for infinitely many }n\ge1.$$
The time unit is the frame time $[t]=\tau$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), so
"infinitely many $n$" means infinitely many returns at unit time steps.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and let $E(q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v+U(q)$ be the energy of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]. If $q:I\to\Omega$ is a $C^2$ solution of the mechanical system $M(q)q''=\tfrac12\nabla_q(q'^{\mathsf T}M(q)q')-(D_qM(q)[q'])q'-\nabla U(q)$ on the interval $I$, then

$$\frac{d}{dt}E\bigl(q(t),q'(t)\bigr)=0\qquad(t\in I);$$

that is, the energy is constant along every solution.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Let $t_0<b$ be reals, let $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, and let $x:[t_0,b)\to\mathbb R^n$ be a solution of the initial value problem

$$x'(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad x(t_0)=x_0$$

on $[t_0,b)$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]). Suppose there is a compact set $K\subseteq D$ and a real $\delta>0$ such that

$$\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\in K\qquad\text{for every }t\in(b-\delta,b).$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a solution $\tilde x:[t_0,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ of the same initial value problem with $\tilde x(t)=x(t)$ for all $t\in[t_0,b)$; in particular $\tilde x(b)=\lim_{t\uparrow b}x(t)$ exists and lies in the state projection of $K$;
2. if moreover $D=\mathbb R\times U$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $F$ is autonomous, $F(t,z)=G(z)$ with $G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]), and if there is a compact $K_0\subseteq U$ with $x(t)\in K_0$ for every $t\in(b-\delta,b)$, then the extension conclusion of clause 1 holds as well.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

derivations.claim: Compactness and phase volume: $E$ is continuous and $A_{E_1}=E^{-1}((-\infty,E_1])$ is closed; if $(x,v)\in A_{E_1}$ then $\tfrac14\lVert x\rVert_2^4\le E_1$ and $\tfrac12\lVert v\rVert_2^2\le E_1$, so $\lVert x\rVert_2\le(4E_1)^{1/4}$ and $\lVert v\rVert_2\le\sqrt{2E_1}$; hence $A_{E_1}$ is contained in the box of side lengths $2(4E_1)^{1/4}$ (three position coordinates) and $2\sqrt{2E_1}$ (three velocity coordinates), is bounded and closed, therefore compact, and by [L3] has dimensionless coordinate Lebesgue volume $\lambda_6(A_{E_1})\le(2(4E_1)^{1/4})^3(2\sqrt{2E_1})^3=512\,E_1^{9/4}<\infty$; it is nonempty because $(0,0)\in A_{E_1}$.

Invariance: along a maximal solution of the quartic model the energy is constant by [L2], so the solution stays in $A_{E_1}$; because $A_{E_1}$ is compact and contained in the state domain $W$, [L2] also shows the solution is defined for all times, and applying the same argument to the reversed motion gives $\Phi_t(A_{E_1})\supseteq A_{E_1}$ as well; hence $\Phi_t(A_{E_1})=A_{E_1}$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$.

Recurrence conclusion: $A_{E_1}$ is a bounded Borel set of finite measure with closure in the flow domain and is invariant by step 2.1; [L1] therefore gives, for every Borel $E\subseteq A_{E_1}$, that almost every state of $E$ returns to $E$ at infinitely many positive integer times.

Failure of the hypothesis for the flat model: for $U\equiv0$, $E_0(x,v)=\tfrac12\lVert v\rVert_2^2$ and the sublevel $\{E_0\le E_1\}=\mathbb R^3\times\{v:\lVert v\rVert_2\le\sqrt{2E_1}\}$ is unbounded, indeed it meets every translate of the velocity ball in the position directions; the phase domain $W=\mathbb R^6$ has infinite Lebesgue measure, so [L1]'s boundedness and finite-measure hypotheses fail. For the motion through $(0,e_1)$, $x(t)=te_1$: if a fixed bounded phase set has $\lVert x\rVert_2\le R$ on it, this trajectory can be in the set only for $0\le t\le R$. It eventually exits and makes only finitely many integer-time visits; this does not claim that no finite return occurs. The finite-volume hypothesis is a genuine restriction.
